procedural_history.originating_court: Court of the Special Judge, Bharatpur, Rajasthan
procedural_history.impugned_order: The petitioner (Gurcharan Dass Chadha) sought a transfer of a criminal case (No. 2 of 1964--State v. Gurcharan Dass Chadha I.P.S.) from the Court of the Special Judge, Bharatpur, Rajasthan to another criminal court of equal or superior jurisdiction subordinate to a High Court other than the High Court of Rajasthan.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The petitioner had filed a writ petition in the High Court of Rajasthan (No. 794 of 1964) which he subsequently withdrew on December 23, 1964 before filing the present petition in the Supreme Court.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The petitioner approached the Supreme Court under s. 527 of the Code of Criminal Procedure seeking the transfer of his criminal case out of Rajasthan, alleging apprehension of unfair trial due to the hostility and influence of certain state officials. While the petition was pending, the State Government served the petitioner with a notice and charge sheet, which led to a separate contempt petition in the Supreme Court.

directions: The transfer of the case from the special Judge, Bharatpur is declined.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court has the jurisdiction under Section 527 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to transfer a case pending before a Special Judge appointed under the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1952.

facts: A public servant was being tried by a Special Judge in Bharatpur, Rajasthan, under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1952.
The public servant petitioned the Supreme Court under Section 527 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) to transfer the case to another state.
The State of Rajasthan opposed the petition, arguing that the Supreme Court lacked the jurisdiction to transfer a case assigned to a Special Judge under the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1952.
law: The State's argument was that the Criminal Law Amendment Act is a special, self-contained law.
Section 7(2) of this Act specifies that an offence must be tried by the Special Judge for the area in which the offence was committed.
The State contended that this specific requirement was inconsistent with the general power of transfer under Section 527 of the CrPC, and therefore, the special law should prevent the transfer.
The Court considered Section 8(3) of the Act, which states that the provisions of the CrPC apply unless they are inconsistent with the Act.
application: The Supreme Court determined that the core question was whether Section 527 of the CrPC was inconsistent with Section 7(2) of the Act.

The Court concluded there was no inconsistency. It distinguished between two conditions in the Act: the first, that the trial *must* be before a Special Judge, which is an essential condition (a sine qua non); and the second, that the trial should be before the Special Judge of the area where the offence was committed.

The Court characterized the second condition (territorial jurisdiction) as being on par with the normal distribution of work among different judges. It held that the power of transfer under the CrPC is specifically intended to overcome such territorial limitations when the ends of justice require it.

Therefore, the Court reasoned that the general power of transfer, which is preserved by Section 8(3) of the Act, must supervene and cause the specific territorial rule of Section 7(2) to "yield". The two provisions operate in different spheres and do not create a contradiction.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that it does have the jurisdiction and power under Section 527 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to transfer a case from a Special Judge subordinate to one High Court to another Special Judge subordinate to another High Court.

issue.issue_text: Whether the petitioner's apprehension of interference with the course of justice was reasonable and sufficient to warrant a transfer of the case on its merits.

facts: The petitioner, a member of an All India Service, was being prosecuted in the court of the Special Judge, Bharatpur, Rajasthan.
He sought to transfer the case out of Rajasthan, claiming he had a reasonable apprehension that he would not receive a fair and impartial trial.
His apprehension was based on the alleged hostility and influence of high-ranking officials, including the then Law Minister and two Deputy Inspector Generals of Police.
The petitioner cited past incidents and differences with these officials as the basis for his fear that they would interfere with the trial.
law: The Court outlined the well-settled law for transferring a case: a transfer is granted if a party has a 'reasonable apprehension' that justice will not be done.
A petitioner does not need to prove that justice will inevitably fail, but must show circumstances that make their apprehension reasonable.
A mere allegation or a 'general feeling' that some persons are hostile is not sufficient.
The court must objectively determine if the apprehension is reasonable, not just that the petitioner genuinely entertains it.
application: The Court applied these legal principles to the petitioner's claims.
It acknowledged that the petitioner might genuinely entertain an apprehension due to past events in his official life and hostility from certain officials.
However, the Court found his apprehension was not 'reasonable' in the legal sense.
The key reason was the petitioner's failure to show any evidence of actual interference, either direct or indirect, with the investigation or the ongoing trial.
The Court noted that the petitioner's allegations were all based on past events and did not demonstrate any current or likely interference with the course of justice.
Furthermore, the petitioner had not made any allegations against the special judge who was actually trying the case.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the petitioner's apprehension, being based only on a general feeling of hostility from certain officials without any evidence of interference in the judicial process, was not reasonable. Therefore, it was not sufficient to warrant a transfer of the case, and the petition was dismissed.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court has the jurisdiction under Section 527 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to transfer a case pending before a Special Judge appointed under the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1952.
appellant_arguments: The petitioner argued that the Supreme Court has the power to transfer the case, invoking its jurisdiction under Section 527 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
respondent_arguments: The State Government (Advocate General) argued that the Supreme Court lacks jurisdiction to transfer a case assigned to a Special Judge under the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1952.

They contended that the Act is a self-contained special law and that under its provisions (specifically Section 7), such offenses must be tried only by the Special Judge for the area where the offense was committed, making the case non-transferable.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the petitioner's apprehension of interference with the course of justice was reasonable and sufficient to warrant a transfer of the case on its merits.
appellant_arguments: The petitioner argued for a transfer based on the apprehension that the State Government was interfering with the course of justice.

This claim was supported by the fact that while the transfer petition was pending, the State Government served the petitioner with a charge-sheet, which the petitioner viewed as an act of indirect pressure and duress intended to hamper the prosecution of his petition.
respondent_arguments: The State Government initially joined issue on the facts and merits of the claim for transfer.
In response to the allegation of pressuring the petitioner with a charge-sheet, the Government of Rajasthan and its Secretary apologized and showed 'proper contrition' for their actions.

cases.case_name: Ramchandra Prasad v. State of Bihar
cases.principle: A transfer of a case by the High Court to a special judge who had no jurisdiction in the area where the offence was committed was valid. This was because Section 8(3) of the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1952, preserves the application of provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure (like transfer powers) so long as they are not inconsistent with the Act.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The Supreme Court, in exercising its power under Section 527 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, can transfer a case from a special judge subordinate to one High Court to a special judge subordinate to another High Court. Statutory provisions that confer territorial jurisdiction on courts are not inconsistent with this power of transfer, as the transfer order itself invests the transferee court with jurisdiction it would otherwise lack.
obiter: A mere allegation of apprehension that justice will not be done is insufficient for a transfer; the court must find that the apprehension is reasonable.
It is a principle of the administration of justice that justice should not only be done but should also be seen to be done.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Although the Court affirmed its jurisdiction to transfer a case from a Special Judge, it dismissed the petition on its merits. The petitioner's apprehension of not receiving a fair trial was deemed unreasonable because it was based on a general feeling of hostility and past events in his official life, with no specific evidence of direct or indirect interference with the ongoing investigation or the trial itself. The State's improper act of pressuring the petitioner during the transfer proceedings was noted but considered remedied by a formal apology.
legal_tests_applied: A mere allegation that there is apprehension that justice will not be done in a given case does not suffice. The Court has further to see whether the apprehension is reasonable or not.

To judge of the reasonableness of the apprehension the State of the mind of the person who entertains the apprehension is no doubt relevant but that is not all. The apprehension must not only be entertained but must appear to the Court to be a reasonable apprehension.
why_appellant_lost: The petitioner's apprehension that he will not receive justice in the State of Rajasthan was found to be not reasonable.

All the facts which he has narrated bear upon past events in his official life. Nothing has been said which will show that there is in any manner an interference direct or indirect with the investigation of the offences alleged against him or the trial of the case before the special Judge, Bharatpur.

A general feeling that some persons are hostile to the petitioner is not sufficient. There must be material from which it can be inferred that he entertains an apprehension and that it is reasonable in the circumstances alleged.
The petitioner did not allege anything against the special Judge who is trying the case.
why_respondent_won: The court found no trace of evidence in the petition or arguments that anyone was interfering or likely to interfere either directly or indirectly with the course of justice.

While the State's action of serving a charge-sheet during the pendency of the petition was deemed an 'indirect pressure' and 'to be deprecated', the Government of Rajasthan and its Secretary 'made amends by proper contrition' and the court accepted their apology, thus neutralizing this specific ground for transfer.
policy_considerations: It is one of the principles of the administration of justice that justice should not only be done but it should be seen to be done.

A literal interpretation of the condition that a case must be tried by a Special Judge for a specific area, which would prevent any transfer, 'could hardly have been intended' by the legislature, as it would also negate the High Court's power to transfer cases intra-state under Section 526 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

The court strongly deprecated the State's action of serving a charge-sheet on the petitioner while his transfer petition was pending, noting it was 'likely to have hampered the petitioner in prosecuting his petition freely before this Court and would have resulted in obstruction of administration of justice.'
